# Graphics test environments for agents on the testing PC: Fable's answer

Written 2026-11-05 by Fable (claude-fable-5-1) from `env/brief.md` and the chat's three additions of the same day. Paths are relative to the repository; `R` is `build/flow/coordinator/graphics-research`, `S` is `build/research/src`, and `X` is the scratchpad where I cloned sources for reading (virglrenderer at tag `virglrenderer-1.3.0`, `cmspam/winq-emu`, `cmspam/winq-emu-virglrenderer`, `cmspam/winq-emu-qemu`, `magma-gpu/rutabaga_gfx`, `google/gfxstream`, and six files of QEMU `v11.0.0` fetched raw). Each claim carries a mark: [measured] a measurement on the machine recorded in `tonight/`, the brief or `env/win-facts-raw.txt`; [read] read in source or a document, with the place; [inferred] my reasoning from those. I ran nothing on any machine and changed nothing but this file.

## The answer first

* Only one environment on this PC can give a guest Vulkan 1.3 with a swapchain on the RTX today, and it is the one the night's run never tried: native QEMU on Windows under WHPX with a Windows build of virglrenderer's Venus. Upstream virglrenderer has no such build; a fork, WINQ-EMU alpha 10 (QEMU 11.0.0 plus virglrenderer 1.3.0 with about 9,900 changed lines, of which the Venus port is roughly 2,500), has one, tested by its author on an Intel B580 and claimed for NVIDIA without evidence. Its design maps a Vulkan `vkMapMemory` pointer of the host driver straight into the guest's PCI BAR through QEMU's blob subregions and `WHvMapGpaRange`, which is the mechanism Google's gfxstream has used on Windows for years, so it is sound in principle [read]. Whether NVIDIA's Windows driver accepts it for every memory type, in particular the 15.67 GiB device-local host-visible type that the RTX exposes with resizable BAR [measured], is the first thing to measure.
* WSL stays the everyday bed: nested KVM, 6 us per exit, virgl on the RTX through d3d12 for OpenGL and WebGL, as measured. Its Vulkan gap is one kernel option, `CONFIG_UDMABUF`, and it can be closed without touching Windows: build WSL's own kernel tag once to get `Module.symvers`, build `udmabuf` as a module with its `vmap` changed to plain `vmap()` (the WSL kernel has no `vmap_pfn`), and `insmod` it as root. That gives Venus on lavapipe at Vulkan 1.3 with a swapchain one level higher than the Debian VM did, with the guest under KVM instead of TCG. Lavapipe still means a CPU device, so DXVK runs, vkd3d-proton probably runs, and Chromium's WebGPU still takes SwiftShader.
* Hyper-V does not help. A Hyper-V Linux VM with a GPU partition is what WSL already is (dxgkrnl, `/dev/dxg`, Mesa's d3d12 and Dozen) with a kernel of one's own, and `.wslconfig`'s `kernel=` gives that too. Discrete Device Assignment is refused by the hypervisor itself on client editions: Microsoft's page of 2026-02-12 says DDA and GPU-P are not supported on Windows 10 or 11 Pro, and the error client machines get, `0xC035001E`, is `HV_STATUS_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE`, a hypervisor status, not a cmdlet check. The WHPX VPCI functions are documented for Windows 10 20H2 with no edition named, but they allocate through the same VPCI stack, and nobody has published a success on a client edition; a 60-line probe would settle it and needs the Radeon dismounted first, which is the owner's call. Rach2 as a Hyper-V guest has no graphics path at all.
* Agents can share the RTX at process level, as any Windows programs do, up to the limits of VRAM (16 GiB) and of WDDM's scheduler; a hang in one guest costs every GPU user a device loss through TDR, so a hang test must run alone. GPU partitions add nothing for Linux guests here.
* Lavapipe inside the guest (Rach2's own Mesa) is the right default for correctness checks of the API surface, DXVK and vkd3d-proton, because it is deterministic, needs no host and has every feature DXVK wants (shaderInt64 included); it settles nothing about the virtio-gpu transport, the display path, or speed, and under TCG it is slow. Lavapipe on the host behind Venus settles the transport and the swapchain, never the GPU.

## What I checked in the earlier research, and what changed

* `tonight/qemu-wsl.md` on Venus over lavapipe (Vulkan 1.2, no swapchain, udmabuf the only cause): confirmed in Mesa 25.0.7, `S/mesa/src/virtio/vulkan/vn_physical_device.c:402-407` (clamp to 1.2 without synchronization2), `:900-910` (external memory needs the renderer's DRM format modifiers and foreign queue family, "expand support once the renderer can run on non-Linux platforms"), `:953-957` (swapchain needs external memory and sync-file semaphore import), `:990` (synchronization2 needs sync-file semaphore import) [read]. The report's reading holds.
* The brief: "libvirglrenderer-1.dll of 881 KB contains 'venus' once and 'vkr_' never, so its Vulkan renderer is probably not built" [measured]. Consistent with upstream: virglrenderer 1.3.0's `meson.build:91` turns threads off on Windows and `:140` turns video off; the Venus sources use `fork`, `close`, `lseek` and `<linux/udmabuf.h>` (`src/venus/vkr_device_memory.c:52,102,595`, `src/proxy/proxy_server.c:694`) and would not compile for Windows [read]. So stock QEMU on Windows has virgl over ANGLE and no Venus.
* `R/plan.md` decision A and `tonight/codex-review.md:103`: the Debian VM as the Venus host, the custom WSL kernel second. Both missed a third route, the udmabuf module without a kernel swap (below), which the brief's own facts allow: `CONFIG_MODULES=y`, no module signing, no lockdown [measured].
* `round3/comparison.md` F6 ("no nested virtualization") is superseded by the night's measurement; I use the night's numbers.
* The brief's `Get-VMHostPartitionableGpu` listing both GPUs with PartitionCount 32 [measured] contradicts the Microsoft Q&A advisor who says GPU-P on 11 Pro is impossible; the measurement wins, and the gist by ad1107 (last active 2026-06-09, Windows 11 Pro, RTX 4070, Ubuntu 24.04 with dxgkrnl-dkms 6.6) shows a Linux guest reaching the GPU that way [read]. Microsoft's "not supported" means unsupported, not refused, for GPU-P; for DDA it means refused (below).

## Facts established this round

* Microsoft, "Troubleshooting guidance for Hyper-V GPU assignment, partitioning, and passthrough", ms.date 2026-02-12: "DDA and GPU-P aren't supported on desktop-class hardware or client operating systems such as Windows 10 or 11 Pro", "To use DDA to assign GPUs, the host computer has to run Windows Server 2016 or a newer version", "If you want to use GPU-P, the host computer has to run Windows Server 2025 or a newer version", and GPU-P's supported GPUs are the NVIDIA A2 to L40S datacenter parts [read, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/virtualization/troubleshoot-hyper-v-gpu-assignment-partitioning-passthrough-issues].
* Microsoft Q&A 1347364 (2023-08-17): on a Windows 11 desktop, `Dismount-VMHostAssignableDevice -force` and `Add-VMAssignableDevice` both succeed, and the VM fails to start with "Virtual pci Express Port ... Failed to Power on with Error 'A hypervisor feature is not available to the user'. (0xC035001e)" [read]. `0xC035001E` is facility 0x35 (Hyper-V) code 0x1E, `HV_STATUS_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE` in the hypervisor's status table [read from memory of `hvgdk.h`; mark inferred for the exact name]. The dismount succeeds because `-force` dismounts any device, as Microsoft's 2015 blog says [read, web summary].
* `WHvAllocateVpciResource` and `WHvCreateVpciDevice`: "Minimum supported Windows: Windows 10, version 20H2 (x64)", `ProviderId` NULL allocates "an SR-IOV virtual function, a discretely assignable physical function", and `WHvCreateVpciDevice` programs the IOMMU for the device's requester ID [read, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/virtualization/api/hypervisor-platform/funcs/whvallocatevpciresource and .../whvcreatevpcidevice, ms.date 2026-06-08]. No edition restriction is written. QEMU's WHPX backend, upstream and the WINQ fork, has no VPCI code (`grep Vpci target/i386/whpx/` empty) [read].
* The machine: ssh lands in session 0; `vulkaninfo` there lists the RTX (1.4.357, driver 621.1, DISCRETE_GPU) and the Radeon (1.4.315, INTEGRATED_GPU); the RTX has heap 0 of 15.67 GiB device-local and heap 1 of 152.87 GiB system, memory type 4 is DEVICE_LOCAL, HOST_VISIBLE and HOST_COHERENT on heap 0 (resizable BAR is on), types 2 and 3 are host-visible system memory, `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` with 4 KiB alignment, shaderInt64, bufferDeviceAddress, timelineSemaphore, hostQueryReset all true; `VK_KHR_external_memory_win32`, `_semaphore_win32`, `_fence_capabilities`; MSYS2 at `C:/msys64` with a UCRT64 gcc; WSL interop starts Windows programs [measured, `env/win-facts-raw.txt`].
* QEMU on Windows: `ui/egl-helpers.c:712` initialises EGL with `qemu_egl_init_dpy_win32(EGL_DEFAULT_DISPLAY, mode)`, that is ANGLE, and `:654` records `qemu_egl_angle_d3d`; `ui/egl-headless.c` builds on Windows with only its dma-buf scanout under `CONFIG_GBM` (`:81`, `:175`); `hw/display/virtio-gpu-gl.c:127` refuses a display without OpenGL, so `-display none` cannot carry virtio-gpu-gl and `-display egl-headless` is the headless form; `hw/display/virtio-gpu-virgl.c:57` turns the map-fixed hostmem method off on Windows, so each blob is its own `memory_region_init_ram_ptr` subregion (`:222-238`) [read, QEMU v11.0.0 and the fork, identical in these files].
* WINQ-EMU: the fork of virglrenderer differs from `virglrenderer-1.3.0` in 90 files, 9,900 diff lines (`diff -r`), among them `src/venus/vkr_win32_shim.c` (new, 700 lines), `vkr_physical_device.c` (542), `vkr_device.c` (389), `vkr_device_memory.c` (285), `src/proxy/proxy_server.c` (671), `vkr_queue.c` (147), `vkr_ring.c` (94), a new `virgl_video_win32.c` (D3D11 decode) and a new `vkr_descriptor_heap.c`; its QEMU fork differs from `v11.0.0` by 129 lines in `target/i386/whpx/whpx-all.c` and 22 in `hw/display/virtio-gpu-virgl.c`, with `ui/egl-*.c`, `virtio-gpu-gl.c` and `virtio-vga-gl.c` unchanged [measured on the clones]. Its README names Windows 10 or 11 with the Hypervisor Platform, "Any GPU with Vulkan drivers. Intel, AMD, NVIDIA", a Linux guest with Mesa 24.0 or later, BIOS boot ("EFI boot causes a timing issue that tanks Vulkan performance to ~5 FPS"), and its only benchmark on an Intel B580 (SuperTuxKart 410 fps against 226 in WSL2) [read]. No release date is printed; the chat says alpha 10 is of April 2026.
* Mesa's Dozen (`S/mesa/src/microsoft/vulkan/dzn_device.c:63`): `DZN_API_VERSION` is 1.2; on Linux it offers `KHR_external_memory_fd` and `KHR_external_semaphore_fd` and not `KHR_external_fence_fd`, no dma-buf and no DRM modifiers (`:115-121`) [read]. A 2026 WSL build reports 1.2.354 and "not a conformant Vulkan implementation" [read, web summary of a third-party README].
* Linux `udmabuf` (`S/linux/drivers/dma-buf/Kconfig:33`): a bool, "depends on DMA_SHARED_BUFFER, MEMFD_CREATE, MMU"; the WSL kernel has those and not `UDMABUF`, `VMAP_PFN` or `Module.symvers` [measured, brief]. Current `udmabuf.c` maps with `vmap_pfn` in `vmap_udmabuf` [inferred from the 6.12 series; the tree under `S/linux` is older and uses `vmap` of pages, `udmabuf.c:74`].
* gfxstream's host builds for Windows (`host/meson.build:139` adds `VK_USE_PLATFORM_WIN32_KHR`, 20 files under `host/vulkan` carry `_WIN32`) and rutabaga_gfx's changelog says "Builds on Linux/Windows"; QEMU's `virtio-gpu-rutabaga` needs only the `rutabaga_gfx_ffi` dependency (`hw/display/meson.build:86`) and its Wayland socket is optional [read]. crosvm lists WHPX and HAXM as its Windows hypervisors and has a Windows build page (`cargo build --features all-msvc64,whpx`) with no word on gpu on Windows [read, https://crosvm.dev/book/building_crosvm/windows.html].
* Hyper-V GPU-P for Linux guests is community work: dxgkrnl out of tree (`staralt/dxgkrnl-dkms`, 6.6 base; a v4 of "drivers: hv: dxgkrnl" was posted to linux-hyperv in March 2026, not known merged), the host's driver files copied into the guest, OpenGL through Mesa d3d12, no Vulkan result shown [read, the gist and the search summaries].

## Question 1: the environments

The chain column lists the layers from a Rach2 program to the silicon. L1 means the guest's CPU runs one level below Hyper-V (WSL's Linux, a Hyper-V VM, a WHPX partition); L2 one level more (a KVM guest inside WSL); L3 one more. "Rach2 work" is what the plan already has to write for QEMU with virtio-gpu (73-3, 74-3: virtio-gpu with blob, context init, host-visible BAR, syncobj and sync files, dma-buf), which every row below needs; rows name only what they add.

Notes by row.

* A and B. The night's chain and numbers. B's udmabuf module: `udmabuf` depends only on options the WSL kernel has [read]; the module needs `Module.symvers` of the running kernel, so the WSL kernel tag is built once with `/proc/config.gz` as its config (a 20 to 40 minute build on 32 threads [inferred]), then `udmabuf.c` is compiled as `M=` with `CONFIG_UDMABUF=m` and its `vmap_udmabuf` changed from `vmap_pfn` to `vmap()` over the memfd's pages, since `VMAP_PFN` is absent [measured]. `insmod` needs root in WSL, which the owner's accounts have through `wsl.exe -u root`; the device node needs the `render` group or a mode. Lost at each WSL restart; a systemd unit in WSL can reload it. The `.wslconfig` route is one line and a `wsl --shutdown`, which ends every agent's session and leaves the Hyper-V VMs alone [inferred].
* C. Works, measured, and stays the fallback that needs nothing. Its cost is TCG at L3 for everything CPU-heavy and no picture out of the VM.
* D. The stock Windows build has `egl-headless`, which on Windows means ANGLE with no window [read, `egl-helpers.c:712`]. ANGLE's default backend on Windows is D3D11, which gives OpenGL ES 3.1 at most; the `*_vulkan_secondaries` copies shipped beside it [measured, brief] suggest an ANGLE built with a Vulkan backend, selectable with `ANGLE_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=vulkan`, which gives ES 3.2 on NVIDIA's Vulkan [inferred]. virgl's guest GL then follows the host GLES as it did on d3d12 (4.2 and ES 3.1 there). In session 0 there is no desktop, but D3D11 and Vulkan devices open there (vulkaninfo did [measured]); whether ANGLE's EGL initialises in session 0 is the first thing D measures.
* E. How a blob reaches the guest in the fork, read in `X/winq-emu-virglrenderer`: `vkAllocateMemory` of a host-visible type is forced to export, with the handle type remapped from OPAQUE_FD to OPAQUE_WIN32 when the host has `VK_KHR_external_memory_win32` (`vkr_device_memory.c:376-398`); `vkr_device_memory_export_blob` gets the NT handle with `vkGetMemoryWin32HandleKHR` and wraps it as a token fd (`:733-760`), skipping the dma-buf size check (`:777`); QEMU's `virtio_gpu_virgl_map_resource_blob` calls `virgl_renderer_resource_map`, which on the in-process path imports the handle into the allocator device and `vkMapMemory`s it (`src/virglrenderer.c:1293`), and wraps the pointer in `memory_region_init_ram_ptr` under the hostmem BAR (`virtio-gpu-virgl.c:222-238`); WHPX's memory listener then calls `WHvMapGpaRange` on that pointer. So the guest sees the driver's own mapping. The render server is in-process threads instead of a forked worker (`proxy_server.c:683-778`, `meson.build:393`). Sync: the guest's sync-file fences and semaphores become OPAQUE_WIN32 fence and semaphore handles (`vkr_queue.c:565-587`, `vkr_win32_shim.c:332-471`), and the host advertises `VK_KHR_external_fence_fd` and `_semaphore_fd` to the guest when it has the win32 forms (`vkr_physical_device.c:361-366`), so Mesa's gate for synchronization2, hence 1.3, passes [read, `vn_physical_device.c:990`]. The dma-buf shim synthesises `VK_EXT_external_memory_dma_buf` and `VK_EXT_image_drm_format_modifier` with LINEAR as the only modifier (`vkr_physical_device.c:405-456`), which Mesa's external-memory gate asks for together with `EXT_queue_family_foreign` (`vn_physical_device.c:903-905`); the renderer passes that one through from the host when the host has it (`vkr_common.c:187`, the table of extensions it allows), and NVIDIA's Windows driver on the RTX does list `VK_EXT_queue_family_foreign` [measured, `win-facts-raw.txt:1369`; the Radeon too, `:3297`]. So all three pieces of the swapchain gate should be present; E2's full vulkaninfo confirms it rather than assumes it. What reaches Rach2 then: `apiVersion` is the minimum of the host's (1.4.357), Venus's own maximum and the renderer's XML version (`vn_physical_device.c:395`), so 1.3 or 1.4; device type discrete; the host's extensions minus what Venus filters; memory types including type 4. What it needs from the guest beyond upstream Venus: nothing, the guest side is unchanged Mesa; its README's Mesa 24.0 floor is for Venus itself [read]. Two risks only measurement settles: whether `WHvMapGpaRange` accepts a pointer into NVIDIA's mapping of the BAR (type 4) as it does system memory (types 2 and 3); the fork was proven on an Intel B580, whose driver also exposes a device-local host-visible type, which is weak evidence it works, and the Android emulator's gfxstream on Windows has mapped NVIDIA host-visible memory into guests for years, which is good evidence for the system-memory types [inferred]. And `IA32_PAT` sync, which the fork added because guest write-combining of the BAR mapping otherwise falls back to uncached, a "perf cliff for virtio-gpu / Venus shared mappings" (fork README) [read].
* E and the project's WHPX patch. The fork's CPUID exit returns the hypervisor's `DefaultResultRax..Rdx` for every leaf (`whpx-all.c:1912-1935` of the fork) where upstream returns QEMU's computed values and takes the hypervisor's RBX only for leaf 0xD subleaves 1 and 2; the project's 15-line patch (`tools/setup/qemu-whpx/whpx-live-xsave-size.patch`) adds subleaf 0 to upstream's special case. The fork's change subsumes the bug: the live RBX is what it returns. No conflict in the files; a conflict in behaviour: the fork's guest sees the host's CPUID whatever `-cpu` says, so `-cpu max,...enforce=on` of the runner (`tools/etude/qemu_profile.c`) no longer filters features, which is acceptable for a graphics bed and not for the release runner, which keeps its own build. The two builds can live in two private prefixes under `build/`.
* F. gfxstream is the second Windows-capable Vulkan transport and the only one with a production history on Windows hosts (the Android emulator). It costs a Rust toolchain on Windows, `rutabaga_gfx_ffi`, and a gfxstream guest driver in Rach2's Mesa besides Venus (Mesa 25.0.7 has `src/gfxstream`, `meson_options.txt:209`), which needs the same virtio-gpu base plus `VIRTGPU_PARAM_CREATE_GUEST_HANDLE` and friends [read]. Worth trying only if E fails on NVIDIA.
* G. A GPU partition gives a Linux VM exactly what WSL has (dxgkrnl, `/dev/dxg`, d3d12 GL, Dozen if built); the VM's own kernel brings udmabuf, which B brings to WSL more cheaply. Not worth the owner's Hyper-V change.
* J. Dozen in WSL is a way to put the RTX behind Venus without Windows, at Vulkan 1.2 and no swapchain, since Dozen on Linux lacks fence fds and dma-bufs [read, `dzn_device.c:115-121`]. Its one merit: Venus relays the host device type, so Dawn would see a discrete adapter; at 1.2 and non-conformant it is a curiosity, not a bed.
* K. VMware Workstation 17 gives Linux guests OpenGL 4.3 through vmwgfx and Mesa svga and no Vulkan [read, Mesa docs]; VirtualBox less. Rach2 would need an SVGA3D driver. Out.

## Question 2: Hyper-V against QEMU, and DDA on Pro

* "Better" has three senses here. Exit cost: WSL's nested KVM gives a guest 6 us per exit at L2 [measured]; a WHPX guest is at L1 but every exit QEMU handles crosses to user mode through the VID driver, which one instrumented report puts at about 3 us for memory exits and 51 us for CPUID exits [read, epkg analysis, uncontrolled]; the project's own whole run was fastest under WHPX (5432 s against 8815 s in WSL, but that WSL run was TCG before nested virtualization) [read, `dev-log/62-etude/machines.md:75`]. So neither is known slower; measure both with one port-I/O loop (run E3 below). GPU reach: a Hyper-V VM reaches the RTX only through GPU-P's dxgkrnl, which is WSL's path; QEMU on Windows reaches it through the host's native Vulkan and D3D11, which is the shortest chain on this PC. Isolation: a Hyper-V VM or WSL cannot hang Windows's GPU driver except through dxgkrnl; a QEMU process on Windows uses the driver as any program does and can trigger a TDR.
* DDA: Pro is refused by the hypervisor. Evidence: Microsoft's page (above); the client-edition error `0xC035001E` at VM start after the cmdlets succeeded [read, Q&A 1347364]; `HV_STATUS_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE` is the hypervisor's own status for a partition without the privilege [inferred from the status table]. The cmdlets exist on Pro because the Hyper-V module is one package; `Get-VMHostAssignableDevice` empty [measured] says nothing is dismounted, not that DDA works.
* The WHPX VPCI functions: documented for 20H2 x64 with no edition named [read]; they allocate a "discretely assignable physical function" through the same VPCI stack that the cmdlets use, so the same partition privilege applies [inferred]. I found no report of anyone calling them for a GPU on any edition. A probe would be a 60-line C program: `WHvCreatePartition`, `WHvAllocateVpciResource(NULL, 0, &desc, sizeof desc, &h)` with a `WHV_SRIOV_RESOURCE_DESCRIPTOR` naming the Radeon's PnP instance path, then `WHvCreateVpciDevice`. The allocation needs the device dismounted from the host first (`Dismount-VMHostAssignableDevice -Force` on `PCIROOT(0)#PCI(0801)#PCI(0000)`, reversible with `Mount-VMHostAssignableDevice`), so it is the owner's call; expected result `ERROR_NOT_FOUND` or `0xC035001E` [inferred]. Low priority: the Radeon assigned to a Linux VM would give Vulkan 1.3 on an iGPU with AMD's open driver, a real second GPU bed, but only if the hypervisor allows it, and I expect it does not.

## Question 3: assigning a GPU

* If DDA worked: the Radeon to a Linux VM is the likelier of the two. The RTX drives the desktop session and dwm [measured], so dismounting it blanks Windows, and the other project's VMs keep running headless but the owner loses the console; the Radeon has no display attached and no session. An iGPU under DDA is the harder case technically (no ROM of its own, shared memory controller, reset by function-level reset only if the firmware allows), and AMD iGPUs under VFIO on Linux hosts are known to need a reset quirk; a headless assignment needs no ROM since the guest's amdgpu initialises without a VBIOS only on some parts. What is gained: a Linux VM with RADV at Vulkan 1.3 and a dma-buf-capable driver, a Venus host that gives guests everything the Lenovo cannot, and a kernel we control. What is lost: Windows's fallback display if the RTX is ever taken. All moot on Pro as far as the evidence goes.
* The RTX to a VM and the Radeon left to Windows: Windows would have to switch its session to the Radeon, which needs a display or the virtual display driver on it and a reboot; a bigger change for a feature the hypervisor refuses.

## Question 4: sharing a GPU

* Process level on the Windows host: each QEMU is a process with a Vulkan or D3D11 device; WDDM time-slices the engines among processes and the driver keeps each context's memory; this is how every game and browser share the RTX. Limits: VRAM, 16 GiB for all guests together, each `hostmem=` window only reserves guest address space, not VRAM; CPU for the renderer threads; the WHPX partitions, which the test runner already runs in numbers. Five accounts with two or three graphics guests each, say 12 QEMUs, is well inside what the host can run; what they contend for is VRAM and the single GPU's time [inferred].
* Hangs: a guest that makes the GPU time out triggers TDR after 2 s; Windows resets the engine or the adapter, and every process whose allocations the reset touches loses its device, including the desktop's compositor [read, Microsoft TDR pages]. So a GPU hang test, or any test that may hang, must run alone and must expect to kill the neighbours' Venus devices. Inside WSL (rows A, B), a hang reaches the host through dxgkrnl and the same TDR applies to the d3d12 contexts.
* Partitions: GPU-P divides the GPU among VMs with the driver's paravirtualization; it is a path for Windows and Linux VMs, not for QEMU guests, and offers no isolation that process sharing lacks on a consumer driver [inferred]. Not useful here.
* Lavapipe shares by CPU: 32 threads, the suites already load 8 of them under TCG [measured]. Each lavapipe instance takes the threads it is given; `LP_NUM_THREADS` caps it; deterministic output.

## Question 5: lavapipe

* Inside the guest, Rach2's own lavapipe (Mesa's lavapipe on Rach2's libc, CPU only) settles: Vulkan 1.4 API conformance of the stack above the driver, DXVK and vkd3d-proton correctness (lavapipe has shaderInt64 and the rest; Wine's vkd3d runs its suite on llvmpipe with some failures allowed [read, vkd3d MR 271]), Chromium's WebGPU only with SwiftShader since Dawn demotes CPU adapters, and the software presentation path through Rach2's DRM. It never settles the virtio-gpu transport, blob mapping, host fences, the real swapchain, or any speed. Deterministic: same picture every run, pixel-exact comparison possible. Under TCG it is slow (10 to 20 times native for CPU-bound code [inferred from the night's boot ratios]); under KVM in WSL it runs at host speed and competes with the suites for the 32 threads.
* On the host behind Venus (rows B, C), lavapipe settles the transport: blobs, host-visible mapping, sync files, the swapchain through the host compositor path, DXVK on Venus; it is still a CPU device to Dawn. It does not settle GPU behaviour (memory types, image modifiers, driver limits, performance).
* Default for agents: lavapipe in the guest for correctness and determinism; Venus over the host lavapipe (B once udmabuf is in) for the transport; Venus over the RTX (E) for what only a GPU shows: WebGPU on a discrete adapter, DXVK and vkd3d-proton at speed, driver limits, Vulkan 1.3 and 1.4 feature queries, and a presented picture.

## Question 6: outside the box

* The udmabuf module in WSL (row B): no Windows change, no WSL restart, a one-time kernel build, a 30-line patch. The cheapest step with the largest gain over today.
* Venus on Windows (row E) as the GPU bed, built privately under `build/` the way `tools/setup/qemu-whpx` already builds a private QEMU with pinned UCRT64 archives: extend `pins.json` with `vulkan-headers`, `vulkan-loader`, `libepoxy`, `python-yaml`, and build the fork's virglrenderer and QEMU in that prefix. No pacman on the machine. If the fork fails on NVIDIA, its Venus port is 2,500 lines on a 1.3.0 base we can read; porting those commits onto upstream head is a task an agent can do.
* `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` on the RTX [measured] allows the reverse mapping: the host imports guest RAM (QEMU's memfd-backed RAM) into Vulkan as device memory with 4 KiB alignment. Venus does not use it today; a guest-allocated blob (`BLOB_MEM_GUEST`) could then be a Vulkan buffer without any BAR mapping, which removes the `WHvMapGpaRange` question for buffers, not images. A later idea, not a task now.
* A Linux host for the second GPU bed: a small machine with a used GPU (a Radeon RX 6600 class card, about 150 to 200 USD used, or a Radeon-equipped mini PC) under Debian with KVM gives Venus on RADV at L1 with real dma-bufs and native-context later, which this PC can give only through row E; it also decouples GPU hangs from the testing host. Or rented: a bare-metal or nested-virt-capable Linux box with a consumer GPU at about 0.5 to 1 USD an hour; agents would reach it over ssh as they reach the Lenovo. Money is the owner's call; the work is the same `tools/setup` enrolment as any machine.
* A different split: most of milestones 73 to 77 is userland (Mesa, Weston, browsers, Wine) on a Linux-compatible interface. Agents can run that userland on WSL itself with the same Debian binaries and Mesa's d3d12 and Dozen before Rach2 boots it, and only the kernel side needs a VM. The environment question then has two answers: WSL for userland, the guest beds for kernel and transport.
* Not worth it: Hyper-V GPU-P VMs (row G), DDA (refused), Dozen as a Venus host (1.2), VMware and VirtualBox (a new driver family), crosvm on Windows (same stack as F with a Rust VMM nobody here runs).

## Question 7: recommendation and the next run

In order:

1. WSL with nested KVM, virgl on the RTX, plus udmabuf (row B): the everyday bed. OpenGL and WebGL on the GPU, Vulkan 1.3 and a swapchain on lavapipe, DXVK, vkd3d-proton, all under KVM at L2, driven as today. Checks that go here: everything in 73 and 74 except WebGPU on a GPU adapter and GPU-only Vulkan features; Rach2's own lavapipe for determinism.
2. Native QEMU on Windows with Venus (row E): the GPU bed. Checks that go here: Vulkan 1.3 and 1.4 on a discrete device, DXVK and vkd3d-proton at speed, Chromium's WebGPU on a Venus adapter, a presented Vulkan picture, memory-type and modifier behaviour of a real driver. Shared with the test runner's WHPX use; one or two instances at a time while it is new.
3. The Debian VM in WSL (row C): the fallback that already works, for Venus at L3 under TCG when B is not yet in or an agent needs an isolated host of its own.

The next experiment run, in priority order. Each names the command, the meaning of pass and fail, and what it needs from the owner. E1 and E2 are the native QEMU run the owner asked for.

* E1. Stock QEMU on Windows, virgl over ANGLE, headless, from WSL as `testing`. Copy the night's Debian overlay to an NTFS path (`C:/rach2-gfx/`, since a `\\wsl.localhost` path is slow through 9P and may refuse qcow2 locking [inferred]). Run:

```
'/mnt/c/Program Files/qemu/qemu-system-x86_64.exe' -name gfxwin -machine q35,accel=whpx,kernel-irqchip=off -cpu max -smp 8 -m 8G \
  -device virtio-vga-gl,blob=on,hostmem=4G -display egl-headless \
  -drive file=C:/rach2-gfx/overlay.qcow2,if=virtio,format=qcow2 \
  -netdev user,id=n0,hostfwd=tcp:127.0.0.1:12271-:22 -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=n0 \
  -serial file:C:/rach2-gfx/serial.log -monitor none -qmp tcp:127.0.0.1:12272,server=on,wait=off
```

  Then in the guest `eglinfo -B -p surfaceless`, `glmark2-drm --off-screen -b :duration=2.0 --size 1280x800`, and the Chromium WebGL probe as in the night. Repeat with `ANGLE_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=vulkan` in QEMU's environment. Pass: the renderer string names ANGLE on the RTX and the probe draws read back; the GLES level and the off-screen score against the night's 89 tell what the ANGLE path costs. Fail with "egl: ..." in session 0: ANGLE cannot initialise without a desktop, and E2 must use the same display, so that fact decides the next step. Needs from the owner: nothing; ssh from WSL to the guest reaches `127.0.0.1` of Windows only in mirrored networking mode, otherwise the host's address from `ip route` in WSL; the chat can read `.wslconfig` to say which.
* E2. Venus on Windows. Prepare a private UCRT64 prefix under `build/tests` by the `tools/setup/qemu-whpx` recipe with the extra archives pinned, build `winq-emu-virglrenderer` (`meson setup b --prefix=PREFIX -Dvenus=true -Dvideo=true -Dtests=false`, video on because the fork links its dma-buf shim with it [read, fork README]) and `winq-emu-qemu` (`configure --target-list=x86_64-softmmu --enable-whpx --enable-opengl --enable-virglrenderer --enable-slirp --disable-docs --disable-plugins`). Run E1's line with the new executable, `-cpu host`, `venus=on`, BIOS boot. In the guest, in order: `VN_DEBUG=init vulkaninfo --summary` (pass: GPU0 "Virtio-GPU Venus (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 SUPER)", apiVersion 1.3 or more, DISCRETE_GPU); full `vulkaninfo` (pass: KHR_swapchain, KHR_synchronization2, KHR_external_memory_fd, EXT_external_memory_dma_buf, EXT_image_drm_format_modifier, EXT_queue_family_foreign present; if swapchain is absent, one of the three external-memory pieces did not reach the guest, and `VN_DEBUG=init` names which); a 40-line program that allocates 64 MiB from each HOST_VISIBLE type the device lists, maps it, writes a pattern, reads it back through a buffer copy (pass on types 2 and 3 proves the system-memory mapping; pass on type 4 proves the BAR mapping through `WHvMapGpaRange`; fail on 4 with `VK_ERROR_OUT_OF_DEVICE_MEMORY` or a QEMU log line from `virtio_gpu_virgl_map_resource_blob` means the renderer must hide type 4, a 10-line change in `vkr_physical_device.c`); `cage -- vkcube --c 300` (pass: exit 0, and a screenshot inside the guest with `grim` shows the cube); the night's `d3d11probe` through DXVK with `DXVK_FILTER_DEVICE_NAME=Venus` (pass: feature level 11_1, readback 255 128 0 255); a `d3d12probe` of the same shape through Wine's vkd3d and through vkd3d-proton's DLLs (pass: device created, readback correct); Chromium with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu --ignore-gpu-blocklist --use-angle=vulkan --enable-features=Vulkan --ozone-platform=x11` under Xwayland (pass: `requestAdapter()` returns the Venus adapter with `isFallbackAdapter` false and both passes correct). Needs from the owner: nothing on Windows; about 10 GiB of disk and an hour of build time on the testing PC; the desktop's GPU may reset once if a test hangs it. Measure also Rach2's own boot under this QEMU with the night's command line, for the exit cost.
* E3. Exit cost, WHPX against nested KVM: Rach2's x86-64 image booted with the night's `-nographic` line under the Windows QEMU with `accel=whpx,kernel-irqchip=off` and under WSL's KVM, the serial stamped per line as in `rach2-l2-kvm-1.txt`; the PCI-search segments give the per-exit cost directly (the night: 6 us at L2). Pass is a number; a WHPX cost above 50 us means the GPU bed's command submission needs the fork's 5 ms exit batching and `kernel-irqchip=on`. Needs: nothing.
* E4. udmabuf as a module in WSL. As root in WSL: clone `microsoft/WSL2-Linux-Kernel` at the tag of `uname -r`, `zcat /proc/config.gz > .config`, `make olddefconfig`, build the kernel once for `Module.symvers`, set `CONFIG_UDMABUF=m`, patch `vmap_udmabuf` to `vmap()` of the folio pages, `make M=drivers/dma-buf`, `insmod drivers/dma-buf/udmabuf.ko`, `chgrp render /dev/udmabuf; chmod 660 /dev/udmabuf`. Then as `testing`: the night's QEMU line (KVM, Venus on lavapipe) and `vulkaninfo` in the guest. Pass: apiVersion 1.3 with KHR_swapchain, as the Debian VM gave at L3, now at L2 under KVM; `vkcube` runs; DXVK takes Venus. Fail at `insmod` with a vermagic or symbol error: the kernel build did not match the running one; the `.wslconfig kernel=` route is then the owner's decision A2. Needs from the owner: root in WSL for the insmod (the chat runs it), nothing on Windows.
* E5. WebGPU in the Debian VM on the Venus adapter with a GPU behind it: only after E2 passes, since on lavapipe Dawn's choice is already known.
* E6. DDA and VPCI probe on the Radeon: the dismount, a throwaway Gen 2 VM, `Add-VMAssignableDevice`, `Start-VM`, expected `0xC035001E`, then `Remove-VMAssignableDevice` and `Mount-VMHostAssignableDevice`; and the 60-line WHPX VPCI program against the dismounted device. Needs the owner's yes; a stuck dismount could need a reboot, which interrupts the other project's VMs; last in the order because the answer is nearly known.

What this run leaves out and why: GPU-P VMs (equivalent to WSL), gfxstream on Windows (only if E2 fails on NVIDIA), VMware and VirtualBox (a new driver family for Rach2), the Lenovo (its Linux session is planned elsewhere).

## Framing

The brief asks which environment lets agents check graphics work with the fewest layers. The better framing is two beds, not one: the transport and the kernel side need a VM and are served by WSL plus udmabuf; the GPU-only facts (Vulkan 1.3 on silicon, WebGPU on a discrete adapter, DXVK and vkd3d-proton at speed) need the host's own driver and are served only by native QEMU on Windows with a Windows Venus or gfxstream. Nested virtualization and Hyper-V are not the obstacle; the obstacle is that the only Vulkan drivers inside WSL are software or Dozen, and the only way to the RTX's Vulkan driver is a process on Windows.

## The three claims I am least sure of

1. That `WHvMapGpaRange` accepts NVIDIA's mapping of the device-local host-visible type (type 4) as it accepts system memory; if not, guest allocations from that type fail until the renderer hides it. Inferred from the fork's B580 result and gfxstream's history, measured by E2's memory-type program.
2. That the fork's sync emulation holds on NVIDIA: guest sync files become OPAQUE_WIN32 fences and semaphores, and the guest's fence signalling relies on QEMU polling the renderer; the fork's only benchmark is on an Intel B580, and its alpha 10 notes on `IA32_PAT` and deferred destruction say the path is still being debugged. A wrong sync shows as hangs or stale frames, which E2's vkcube and DXVK readbacks would catch, not as a refused extension.
3. That `0xC035001E` is `HV_STATUS_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE` and that the WHPX VPCI functions meet the same refusal on Pro; the status name is from memory of the hypervisor's status table, and the VPCI path has no published test on a client edition. E6 settles it, at the owner's call.

Also unverified: that ANGLE's EGL initialises in session 0 (E1), that the `*_vulkan_secondaries` ANGLE libraries are a Vulkan backend (E1 with `ANGLE_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=vulkan`), the per-exit cost of WHPX on this machine (E3), and that the WSL kernel tag builds with the running config to a matching `Module.symvers` (E4).
